BEYOND HR: HUMAN CAPITAL GOVERNANCE & CORPORATE ACCOUNTABILITY

When companies rush to adopt AI and cut costs, who protects the employees?

In 2026, automation is driving business decisions faster than ever. But efficiency has an uncomfortable flip side:

Are companies transforming responsibly or are employees quietly paying the price?

• Cost discipline is necessary, but compromising human dignity is not. 
• Behind every restructuring plan, pay cut and AI-driven evaluation is a real person, livelihood and a family. 
• Business transformation should never come at the expense of human fairness.

THE 6 MATERIAL WORKFORCE RISKS
Workforce management is not just an HR issue. It affects corporate risk, reputation and continuity:
Fair Compensation: Pay gaps, delayed wages and inadequate pay erode trust and retention.
Workplace Dignity: Safety, respect and protection from harassment must apply at every level.
Burnout & Attrition: Excessive pressure drives talent away, taking experience and client relationships with it.
Procedural Fairness: Restructuring must be transparent, lawful and empathetic.
Extended Workforce: Contract, gig and vendor workers deserve fair treatment and safe conditions.
Algorithmic Bias: AI in hiring, monitoring and reviews needs human oversight, privacy safeguards and bias checks.

THE 4 GOVERNANCE PILLARS
Leadership must move beyond routine HR administration:
1. Workplace Dignity: Whistleblower channels, accessible grievance mechanisms and protection against harassment.
2. Labor Integrity: Timely wages, fair pay and labor-law compliance across workforce categories.
3. Ethical Automation: Transparent AI, data protection, responsible monitoring and reskilling.
4. Human Capital ROI: Track retention, leadership development, workforce stability and resilience alongside financial performance.

BOARD-LEVEL OVERSIGHT
→ Workforce risks deserve board-level attention alongside financial, cyber and regulatory risks.
→ Boards should ensure:
• Human capital risks are integrated into Enterprise Risk Management (ERM).
• Executive performance reflects retention, workforce stability and culture, not just cost reduction.
• Confidential, retaliation-protected reporting channels enable independent oversight.

✓ Transformation does not mean rejecting automation. It means ensuring innovation respects legal obligations and human fairness.
✓ You can automate workflows and optimize costs, but you cannot outsource responsibility for human dignity.

A QUESTION FOR REFLECTION: When automation or restructuring affects employees, where should leaders draw the line between protecting margins and safeguarding dignity, wellbeing and long-term organizational capability?

Data Centres in Nova Scotia: Opportunity or Long-Term Liability?

The proposed $10 billion data centre investment in Point Tupper has sparked strong opposition. As someone working in technology, I see the value of infrastructure that supports AI and cloud computing. I am not opposed to data centres. But Nova Scotia must do proper due diligence before committing to a project of this scale.

The opportunity
EverWind proposes over $8 billion for a data centre campus and another $2 billion for renewable energy. Its projections include 2,000 construction positions, 215 permanent jobs, $137 million in annual provincial GDP contribution, and $1.5 billion in provincial corporate taxes over 20 years.
For Cape Breton, that could mean contracts for local businesses, more skilled jobs and investment in clean power. But these are projections, not guaranteed returns.

The risks
The campus could require up to 420 MW of electricity. At 90% use, that is roughly 3.31 TWh a year - about 37% of Nova Scotia's total electricity generation in 2023. That raises real questions about grid capacity, power bills and emissions.
The developer also estimates water use of around 500,000 litres daily at full capacity. And while construction employment is substantial, 215 permanent jobs is modest relative to the scale of investment and resources involved.

What should Nova Scotia require?

Protect ratepayers: Make the developer pay the incremental grid and connection costs, with independent oversight so existing customers are not left with the bill.
Assess environmental impacts: Publish independent findings on water, cooling, emissions and cumulative effects.
Enforce clean-energy promises: Set measurable targets and deadlines for additional renewable generation and reliable supply.
Keep value local: Agree on local hiring, training, procurement and public reporting - not just broad job announcements.
Plan for the exit: Require funded guarantees for decommissioning, site restoration and stranded infrastructure if the project closes early.

What is the real return?
The projected $137 million a year in GDP contribution equals about $2.74 billion over 20 years if sustained. But GDP is not tax revenue, and a $10 billion private investment is not $10 billion in direct benefits to Nova Scotians. The province should publish an independent, long-term cost-benefit assessment, including public costs and risks.
I believe Nova Scotia should welcome serious AI infrastructure investment - but only on terms that protect residents for decades, not just during construction.

The question is not whether we want data centres. It is what conditions make them worthwhile for Nova Scotia.

"What do I actually tell a developer?"

That is the #1 question non-technical founders and industry experts get stuck on when they have a serious software idea.

And if you hire a traditional consultant to help you answer it, they usually hand you a 30-page PDF filled with database diagrams and technical jargon you can't read.

The problem? You can't "feel" a PDF. You can't hand a static document to a colleague, a patient, or an early client and watch where they get confused.

When I designed, built, and deployed my own SaaS platform (Tomeer) from scratch, I didn't start by writing production code. I used an AI-accelerated architecture and prototyping workflow to pressure-test the exact user journey first.

Today, I run that exact same 3-step process for non-technical domain experts inside our Product Clarity Sprint:

• Week 1: Diagnose the Workflow. We strip away the noise, map the security and compliance requirements, and define the leanest MVP worth building.

• Week 2: Prove It with a Clickable Prototype. I build a working, interactive prototype you can actually click through on your screen. The plan is the product; the prototype is the proof. It lets you feel the workflow and validate it before you commit major capital.

• Week 3: The Build-Ready Plan & Cost Estimate. You leave with a complete technical specification, recommended tech stack, phased rollout plan (MVP vs. Phase 2), and a grounded cost estimate for the full build—so you know what to budget before hiring a dev team.

Best of all: we don't lock you in. The roadmap and prototype are yours to take to any developer, and if you choose to build with NRTech, your entire Sprint fee is credited toward your development contract.

Have an app idea you've been sitting on because you don't want to gamble with a dev shop? Let's test the blueprint first.

Japan’s Supreme Court Is Hiring a Digital Transformation (DX) Professional: A Sign of Accelerating Business Process Reform in the Public Sector

The Supreme Court of Japan has announced a recruitment initiative for a DX professional responsible for developing business automation tools and supporting business process reform (BPR).

What makes this recruitment particularly noteworthy is that the role goes beyond introducing IT systems or digitizing existing workflows. It explicitly includes reviewing, redesigning, and fundamentally improving the way work is performed.

■ Position Overview

* Position: DX Promotion Specialist (Business Automation Tool Development and Business Process Reform Support)
* Workplace: Supreme Court of Japan and Tokyo High Court
* Number of positions: One
* Employment status: Full-time fixed-term national government employee
* Contract period: Three years starting April 2027, with the possibility of an extension of up to two additional years
* Annual salary: Approximately JPY 8.2–9.5 million

■ Two Key Areas of Responsibility

1. Business Automation and Efficiency Improvement

Develop, implement, and maintain business applications and automation tools using Microsoft 365, low-code platforms such as Power Apps, and RPA solutions such as Power Automate and UiPath.

2. Business Process Reengineering (BPR)

Identify operational challenges and redesign existing workflows from a DX perspective. Importantly, this includes not only automation but also eliminating unnecessary tasks, simplifying processes, and implementing fundamentally better ways of working.

■ What Kind of Talent Is the Supreme Court Looking For?

In addition to hands-on experience with low-code development or RPA implementation, candidates are expected to demonstrate the ability to analyze business challenges, identify stakeholders’ underlying needs, and translate those needs into practical solutions.

Preferred experience includes:

* BPR and business transformation in large-scale organizations
* Using generative AI to improve operational efficiency and automation
* Leading IT projects from planning and analysis through implementation and adoption
* Translating business challenges into IT requirements
* Agile development and enterprise-wide project leadership
* Driving organizational change and embedding new ways of working

What stands out is the emphasis not merely on technical expertise, but also on the ability to understand business operations, engage stakeholders, and ensure that transformation is successfully implemented and sustained.

■ My Takeaway: DX Is Ultimately About Transforming How Organizations Work

The essence of digital transformation is not simply replacing existing processes with digital tools.

It is about fundamentally rethinking business processes, eliminating unnecessary activities, and leveraging new technologies to transform how organizations create value.

The fact that Japan’s highest judicial institution is seeking to recruit professionals with practical BPR and DX experience from the private sector is particularly significant.

It reflects the growing recognition that even large, complex public institutions need to bring in external expertise and accelerate operational transformation from within.

The next generation of DX professionals will need more than the ability to use technology. They will need the ability to transform the way organizations work.

How do you see the growing role of private-sector DX talent in public institutions?

LEAN HEAVY ON YOUR NETWORK.
Looking for a job? Retiring from the military? Contract ending in January? Thinking about changing careers?
Here's some advice.
1. LEAN HEAVY ON THE NETWORK YOU ALREADY HAVE.
First, turn on that #OpenToWork banner. Let people know you're available.
Update your resume. Use AI to help tailor it to specific positions. Just make sure it's accurate and actually represents your experience.
Then start reaching out to people you know.
Send your buddy a message:
"Hey Tom, I'm retiring in a few months and starting to look for opportunities in the defense industry. I've attached my resume. If you hear of anything or know somebody who's hiring, would you mind passing it along? Appreciate you, buddy!"
That's it.
You don't need a perfectly polished sales pitch. You need to let people know you're looking.
2. EXPAND YOUR NETWORK.
LinkedIn has a pretty powerful search function. USE IT.
Search your geographic area. Search your industry. Search people with similar technical backgrounds. Find professionals at companies where you'd like to work.
Connect with them.
And when you send a message, make it personal.
"Hey, I noticed you're working in aerospace here in Hampton Roads. I've spent the last 10 years working on radar systems and I'm exploring new opportunities in the field. Thought it would be great to connect!"
That's a real person reaching out for a real reason.
Not another obviously AI-generated networking message that sounds like it was written by a corporate refrigerator.
3. FOLLOW THE RECIPE. AND FOLLOW UP.
Make it easy for people to reach you.
Keep your LinkedIn profile updated. Make sure your contact information is accessible to the people you want hearing from you.
If you're comfortable sharing a professional email address or phone number, give people a way to contact you directly.
And follow up with people. Not every day. Don't become a nuisance.
But don't assume one message is the end of the conversation, either.
Here's the thing.
I've been connecting with a lot of professionals lately, especially people who are #OpenToWork.
Some have reached out to introduce themselves. Some have shared their experience. Some are actively looking for their next opportunity.
And I think that's exactly what LinkedIn is supposed to be about.
You don't have to wait for someone to discover your resume in a stack of 300 applications.
You can make yourself known.
You can build relationships.
You can ask for help.
And when you're in a position to help somebody else, return the favor.
Lean heavy on your network. Expand it. Follow up.
You never know which conversation might open the next door.
And if you're #OpenToWork right now, what kind of opportunity are you looking for?
Let's get some conversations started.

The hiring timeline is broken. When the economy bounces back, the white-collar jobs won't. 📉⚠️

In historical recessions, companies laid off workers during downturns and rehired them when consumer demand returned. But generative and agentic AI have changed corporate scaling models permanently.

Today, when enterprise balance sheets rebound, CFOs aren't approving new headcount requisitions. They are expanding AI software capacity. They absorb increased volume through automated infrastructure at a fraction of the cost.

This creates a Jobless Economic Recovery for knowledge workers—where corporate profits hit record highs while white-collar hiring remains stagnant.

According to data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and macro forecasts:

• The Recovery Paradox: Enterprise firms scale back up post-downturn by expanding AI software capacity, not human headcount. Profit margins recover, but white-collar employment remains flat.
• Software Over Payroll: Deploying agentic workflows costs a fraction of hiring full-time employees (no benefits, payroll tax, or severance). CFOs are mandating technology capital expenditure over labor expansion.
• The W-2 Dependency Risk: Single-salary reliance in an automated corporate structure creates severe long-term vulnerability. Median unemployment duration stretches as traditional corporate re-entry slows.

Do not rely solely on a traditional corporate safety net. It is time to audit your task exposure and pivot your skillset into automation-resistant strategy.

3 Ways to Build Your Defense System:

1. Build 6–12 Month Liquidity: Maintain a lean, high-liquidity financial cushion to manage transitions.

2. Diversify Revenue Streams: Establish fractional consulting, advisory, or secondary contracts.

3. Manage Compute Architecture: Shift from executing manual tasks to directing automated AI workflows.

Don't wait in a line that isn't moving. Audit your exposure today.

Here’s an abbreviated version of my Prelude Music Foundation talk, Tomorrow’s Economy Sings Today. (fair warning: this was intended to be provocative!).
__________
 
A baby girl born today will live into the 22nd Century (life span = 81.4 yrs), & she’ll grow up in a world where learning already happens anytime & anywhere, about anything, from anyone.
 
My mom grew up in a one-stoplight northern Indiana town shaped by a couple state roads & a train track. Corn & soybean country, flourishing in the flattest, most fertile soil in the world. Generational family farmers did the job probably exactly like anyone reading this right now imagines.
 
Yet my friends Boahemaa & AJ teach me that Ag isn’t that Ag anymore. Now? Drones, IoTs, robots, aeroponics, & data science - mining insights from millions of inputs to strengthen crop yield.
 
At the same time, despite the massive educational, economic, and ethical questions we’re struggling to answer right now, AI can scrub a contract for loopholes & spot fractures in bone X rays at warp speed, and ~40,000 robots have popped up in manufacturing.
 
Talk with hiring managers in companies of absolutely any size & industry, and you’ll probably hear what I hear about the requisite skills of today’s economy, including: Creativity. Problem solving. Quirk. (WEF Future of Jobs, 2025) In some ways, this is old news, too. I talked with the Chief Learning Officer of a Fortune 50 (not 500) company nearly 10 years ago who said this:

“If your students aren’t curious, we won’t hire them.”
 
School systems understandably but almost exclusively prioritize Kinder readiness, 3rd & 8th grade reading & math, and some smashup of what some group of people said constitutes “college, career, & military readiness.”
 
Hiring managers demand more.
 
So a couple questions:
1. Where should a community prioritize investments to drive way better outcomes? We’ve known for years the highest rate of return per $1 invested comes early - from prenatal through age 5 (Cameiro & Heckman, 2003).
2. Where can we prioritize efforts to drive outcomes that school systems are held to AND hiring managers demand?
 
The answer might be found in a set of leading indicators that can be developed in our youngest learners: attention, self-regulation, early literacy, early numeracy, belonging, etc.
 
I run an org with at least a couple superpowers: we’re a “systems MRI” – we diagnose systems to figure out what’s really going on, especially when orgs try to improve &/or grow. What’s driving & inhibiting results? And, we can predict “black ice” – what derails progress that we need to plan for (clarity, context, capacity, rigor, risk).
 
So,…as we partner w/ Prelude to grow from serving 3,000 children a week to 10,000, we’re helping them research & identify what’s driving the impact that matters the most so they truly scale excellence.

Huge shoutout to photographer Jose Monterrosa at Imagina Communications (https://lnkd.in/g632GfWK).
